Healthcare Interrupted

By: Stenette Grosskopf | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Many routine, yet essential healthcare services are impacted on by Covid-19

Unique Selling Point:
The world is focussing on Covid-19, and the devastating effects on humanity, but experts are warning that there are other humanitarian crises waiting in the wings. Thousands of people across South Africa depend on regular access to medicine and healthcare, patients with HIV, TB, Diabetes, Heart Disease to name but a few... but Covid-19 is disrupting more and more of the healthcare services that these people depend on. From being harassed by police on their way to the clinic, to being too scared to seek medical help, or to collect medicines... it is becoming evident that we're faced with an imminent disaster.

Summary:
Covid-19 has disrupted our lives in many ways. Businesses have closed, people have lost livelihoods, loved ones... The world as we knew it just a few months ago has changed forever. One important, sometimes overlooked, impact is the disruption in routine medical services across the world. 

Reports from many countries show severe disruption of routine healthcare services in many countries due to lockdowns imposed, diversion of healthcare workforce to COVID-19 response, and disruption of travel and supply chains. Even basic immunization services have come to a grinding halt in many settings.

Internationally the Irish National Breast Screening Programme (Breast Check) reports 0 mammograms for the month of April, and a 96% reduction in samples sent to CervicalCheck labs. In the USA, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association warn that emergency rooms across the country are 40 to 50% less busy when it comes to cardiovascular patients seeking care. People are staying home, ignoring serious symptoms for fear of contracting Covid-19.
New figures from University College London suggest there could be 18,000 more cancer deaths in England because of the coronavirus pandemic.
A similar situation is playing off in Sub-Saharan Africa. Besides cancer and heart disease we have a set of medical challenges that cannot simply be ignored until we find a vaccine for Covid-19.
Prof Sanne (Right to Care) told News24 there had been an increase in missed appointments by HIV patients of between 40% and 60% since the lockdown, and a similar issue was expected for diabetes and other illnesses needing chronic medication.



Further information:
MALARIA
In 2018 there were over 228 million cases of malaria in the world, with around 405,000 deaths. 93% of all cases are in Sub-Saharan Africa. Malaria modelling analysis by the Global Malaria Programme at the WHO estimates that malaria deaths in sub-Saharan Africa in 2020 would reach 769 000, twice the number of deaths reported in the region in 2018. This would represent a return to malaria mortality levels last seen in the year 2000. This is because of disruption to insecticide-treated net campaigns, as well as medical limitations. “Controlling malaria depends on access to essential services, like rapid diagnostic tests, antimalarial drugs, and insecticide-treated bed nets. If any or all of these are disrupted due to COVID-19, whether it’s through campaigns that don’t happen, supply chain interruptions, or people not able to access diagnosis and treatment, decades of progress could be undone in just months,” said Jennifer Gardy, a Deputy Director with the malaria team at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

TB
Tuberculosis is a crisis in South Africa. We have about 400,000 cases annually in SA, and it continues to be the leading cause of death in SA. A TB Modeling Study by the Stop TB Partnership shows that with a three-month lockdown and a protracted 10-month restoration of services, global TB incidence and deaths in 2021 could increase to levels last seen in between 2013 and 2016 respectively, implying a setback of at least five to eight years in the fight against TB. Globally, we could see an additional 6.3 million cases of TB between 2020 and 2025 and an additional 1.4 million TB deaths during that same period.

In South Africa, Prof Madhi reports that there has been a 50% reduction in TB testing since lockdown. So people with the disease are not getting the help they need. There are also reported interruptions in patients getting their medication. Dr Emily Wong is a TB and HIV physician-scientist and supervisor in the Sub-Saharan African Network for TB/HIV Research Excellence (Santhe), based at the Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) in Durban. She warns that patients not regularly taking their medications could lead to an increase in TB-related deaths. And on top of that untreated TB makes a patient even more susceptible to Covid-19.

“Finding and treating people with TB remain the fundamental pillars of TB prevention and care and those would require maintained attention,” says Professor Geoffrey Setswe from the Aurum Institute in Johannebsurg.

Prof Madhi reports that about 30% of people approached by community healthcare workers for Covid-19 testing (In the Community Testing Programme) refuse to be tested. People are scared of being taken away. So someone with onset symptoms for TB is not necessarily keen on being tested (in case it is Covid-19). On top of that, historic practices of forcefully sending patients with drug resistant TB to far away hospitals have also left its mark on communities. It's adding to the fear of being tested.

TB medications are most effective if the disease is caught early, and treatment is not interrupted. Covid-19 poses obstacles for both. 

HIV
Similar to TB, HIV is a major concern for sub-Saharan countries. South Africa has seen the biggest HIV epidemic in the world. 7.7 million people are living with HIV in SA, around 62% is estimated to be on ARV. A six-month interruption of supply of ARVs across the whole population of people living with HIV on treatment would be expected to lead to an approximately 2-fold increase in HIV-related deaths over a one year period compared to the case with no disruption. In sub-Saharan Africa this amounts to an excess of over 500,000 adult HIV deaths (including deaths of TB) should such a high level of disruption occur. The coronavirus pandemic could effectively set the clock on AIDS-related deaths back to 2008, when more than 950000 AIDS-related deaths were observed in the region.

South Africa has made huge strides in the fight against HIV, particularly in recent years, but with Covid-19 in the neighbourhood the country will be forced backwards, and set targets will not be reached.

When treatment is adhered to, a person’s HIV viral load drops to an undetectable level, keeping that person healthy and preventing onward transmission of the virus. When a person is unable to take antiretroviral therapy regularly, the viral load increases, impacting the person’s health, which can ultimately lead to death. Even relatively short-term interruptions to treatment can have a significant negative impact on a person’s health and potential to transmit HIV.

Disrupted services could also reverse gains made in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Since 2010, new HIV infections among children in sub-Saharan Africa have declined by 43%, from 250 000 in 2010 to 140 000 in 2018.

NGO, Right to Care in Johannesburg, (Prof Ian Sanne) says that a high percentage of HIV-positive South Africans are missing their clinic appointments to collect their medication and testing for HIV has also dropped drastically due to fears of contracting Covid-19. The irony is that while people living with HIV really need their medication, they also need to avoid Covid-19 as their HIV status makes them particularly vulnerable. So, the dilemma for patients is whether to venture out on public transport and sit in crowded clinics for medication, or simply stay at home? There are some programmes emerging to help in this regard, Right to Care has designed and prototyped an ATM-like device. The pharmacy dispensing unit (PDU) will enable patients to visit locations that are convenient to them to pick up prescribed medication. All collected medications will be recorded against a central patient record. Some Clinics have also streamline processes to assist patients. Themba Lethu Clinic situated at Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg has reduced the waiting time from 4 hours to 45 minutes for medication, according to Right to Care.

There has also been a dramatic decrease in voluntary male circumcisions, which could accelerate the spread of HIV. Likewise more sporadic use of medication because someone with a higher viral load is more likely to infect another person with HIV.

MATERNAL AND INFANT MORTALITY
Unicef and the John Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health estimate that an additional 1.2 million children under the age of 5 could die because of a disruption in routine services like family planning, childbirth, postnatal care, and vaccinations. 

It is estimated that South Africa's current infant mortality rate is around 25.772 deaths per 1000 live births, and these numbers are significantly lower than in the past. Although SA has a bad track record when it comes to Maternal and Infant mortality, as a country we have made huge strides, specifically in cutting down the transmission rate of HIV infections from Mother to baby. As a country we have improved the health of mothers and babies, but with Covid-19 we could take a huge step backwards.

Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital delivers about 60 babies every day. (According to a Wits University Study) The reality for most pregnant women in Soweto is that they are limited to and dependant on the hospital for all their pre- and postnatal care. Researchers found that while 20–25% of stillbirths occurred due to maternal medical conditions such as hypertension and diabetes, it also found that invasive bacterial infections were the immediate or underlying cause of death in 57.5% of all neonatal deaths. Overall, 74.4% of infection-related deaths were hospital-acquired, mainly due to multidrug-resistant bacteria. And this is all during “normal” times. Add Covid-19 to the mix and the situation begins to look dire for mothers and babies of Soweto.

The economic downturn as a result of Covid-19 also plays a role in the maternal and infant mortality rates. Unicef reports that a one percent decrease in per capita GDP roughly correlates to a 0.3 percent increase in infant mortality, with girls at least twice as likely to be affected.

The Measles and Rubella Partnership has estimated that more than 117 million children in 37 countries will miss out on their chance to be vaccinated for measles because mass campaigns and immunisation services will be suspended.

Doctors Without Borders predict that 253,500 to 1.1 million additional children could die from preventable diseases. For every 1 adult life spared (COVID-19) an estimated 100 children could lose their lives.

DIABETES
Diabetes is another chronic illness that people need a constant medicine supply for, which can easily be disrupted by the health system being overstretched. At the moment there is no reported disruption in insulin supplies, but it difficulties would be inevitable as Covid-19 continues to demand focus from our medical world.
An additional issue with all these chronic diseases is that it also makes the patient more vulnerable to Covid-19 itself. People with HIV and TB are at increased risk of contracting the disease itself, while people with diabetes are not more likely to get COVID-19 than the general population. The problem people with diabetes face is primarily a problem of worse outcomes, not greater chance of contracting the virus. And if your blood sugar levels are not controlled this makes it a lot worse. All the more reason for a steady/uninterrupted supply of medicine and care.  


BUT ITS NOT ALL DOOM AND GLOOM... there are some innovations that are being rolled out to assist patients in accessing their much-needed medications. -- like the Right ePharmacy Solutions, like Smart medicine lockers in key locations, and Pharmacy Dispensing Units (PDU's), which are basically medicine ATM's. -- There are also calls for government to supply patients with 6 months' HIV medication to limit the number of times the patient has to venture out and put himself at risk.

Script:


Healthcare Interrupted




V/O
For six months, the world’s attention has been on COVID-19. But our tunnel-vision-focus on one pandemic means we are sidelining others that have been with us much longer.

Modelling by the World Health Organisation estimates that healthcare disruptions caused by the coronavirus could lead to 500 000 additional AIDS-related deaths between now and next year, with more than a 100% increase in new HIV infections amongst children.
Malaria deaths could double, while the prevention and treatment of TB may be set back 5 to 8 years.
Prof Francois Venter
It's this weird thing in our society where people think all other illnesses have been suspended. People are getting older, they're getting other diseases like cancer and diabetes, they're getting HIV.


V/O
Prof Francois Venter is a veteran of South Africa’s long fight against HIV/AIDS. He has first-hand knowledge of how many decades of frontline research and lobbying lie behind our recent successes.
Prof Francois Venter
We really have made unbelievable gains with the HIV program both in terms of treatment and prevention. The TB programme as well has enjoyed for the first time in decades such success in the last three or four years.
V/O
South Africa is also enjoying hard-won gains in the fight against maternal and neonatal death rates.

But now all this is at risk of being eroded, and we face a looming catastrophe in our already strained healthcare system - one that will cost our embattled economy and divided population dearly.


LINK
Millions of South Africans are on chronic medication for hypertension to HIV, tuberculosis and even diabetes. These people need to diligently take their medication regularly, especially since it’s believed that they are more vulnerable to the coronavirus.
VO
But when the country entered hard lockdown in March, that became easier said than done.
Siyabonga
I’m HIV+ since from birth...
VO
In December, eighteen year-old Siyabonga and his brother fled their abusive home in Limpopo and found refuge here at Soweto-based NGO, iKageng. Only a few months later, things went from bad to worse as the pandemic took hold.
Siyabonga
I tried to go for medication but I didn’t reach for that goal.
Claire: Why?

Because I went here in Mandela Sisulu and I found the other woman, and I tried to explain the story, eish Ma’am I don’t have a transfer from the clinic but I’m looking for at least treatment. The lady replied, no we can’t give you treatment.
VO
In the turmoil of escaping Limpopo, he left behind the documents that would allow him to access his ARV treatment in Gauteng.
Siyabonga
That’s the only thing that I forgot there in Limpopo. I took all the things, even the transfer from the school but I forgot that one.


VO
Siyabonga endured two months without treatment - until iKageng intervened on his behalf in late May.
Dr Bronwyn Bosch
As soon as you're not taking your ARVs the HIV can multiply in the blood and overpower the immune system.
VO
Dr Bronwyn Bosch of Ezintsha explains that although it is different for every patient, treatment disruptions are worrisome.
Bronwyn Bosch
Any interruptions in treatment whether it's a day or a month or a year, the HIV if there is any ARV or be in the blood it can become resistant to those ARVs. So the regimen that you're on may not necessarily work anymore.
V/O



As we entered lockdown, most non-essential medical care was suspended. Specialised clinics were closed, elective surgeries delayed, and services scaled down to ready the system for COVID-19.
But it is becoming clear that lockdown is not the only factor preventing people from accessing healthcare…
Phumzile


I’m scared, because it kills, so I am scared.
VO
Single mother Phumzile Kubheka relies on hypertension medication and ARVs. But for her, the threat of the coronavirus looms larger than her chronic conditions.
Phumzile
If I die after I go to the clinic who will my children be left with, because to them I'm everything. I live alone with them in this house, so yes it is scary.
V/O
Phumzile is not alone. Most healthcare sectors - public and private - are reporting a decrease in patients seeking routine care.
People are staying away from clinics and hospitals, especially the elderly and those with chronic conditions, labelled as “Covid Co-morbidities”, says Gloria Sibeko of iKageng.
Gloria
Even grannies, grannies will stay with such high hypertension knowing very well that I’m not feeling okay.
Prof Francois Venter
We're seeing a dramatic drop in TB testing across the country. And we're seeing a decrease in pick-ups for antiretrovirals.
VO
For those who do seek care, Covid infection control measures can lengthen waiting times.
Phumzile
18:03:37:05

I left my house at 5 o’clock.I went to the clinic and stood there til around 9am.
Gloria
they have to wait out of the clinic, and queue out of, and maintain social distancing…


VO
When it comes to chronic medication at least, there is one solution that minimizes contact, queuing time, and the risk of infection.
Link
When you think of postboxes you think of something from yesteryear but in these challenging times perhaps we should look to the past for inspiration.
VO
Adapting existing technology and innovations, Right ePharmacy is rolling out “Collect and Go” medicine lockers at 70 sites across Gauteng, Mpumalanga and the Free State.
Fanie - Right to Care
They can just basically come to the locker, they put in their unique pin. The locker opens, you take your medicine and you go on with your normal day.
V/O
Right ePharmacy also has ATM Pharmacies, known as PDU’s at various locations in Johannesburg, and in Bloemfontein, explains managing director, Fanie Hendriksz.
Fanie - Right to Care
So the benefits, you can see we’re in a community shopping centre, so people are now aligning their medicine collection with the onthly or weekly or daily shopping. It’s close to a taxi route.
V/O
The units operate 7 days a week and patients connect “real time” with a pharmacist who can advise them if they have any concerns. Behind the interface is a stock room where a robotic arm selects the appropriate medication, labels it and dispenses it to the patient.
Fanie - Right to Care
We’ve seen that the collection time is under 3 minutes - and that means 2 months’ supply and a live interaction with the pharmacist.
V/O
Taking strain off public clinics and hospitals will improve access to treatment for non-COVID patients. But for some services, there’s no avoiding human contact.
Link
Most experts agree that children aren’t as severely affected by Covid-19 directly as adults and the elderly. But the real concern is the indirect repercussions of the pandemic.
Anne Kahts
Dit is baie angstig om uit te gaan, veral met ‘n piep babatjie.

(It is very unnerving to go out, especially with a small infant.)
VO
Anné Kats gave birth to a baby boy at the beginning of May. Navigating lockdown with a newborn has exacerbated the anxiety of being a new mother.
Anné Kahts
Ons was op ‘n deel was ons na ‘n Covid-19 hospitaal toe - wat uitgesit is vir Covid-19 pasiente, want hy moes sy polio drops gaan kry het. Hy was rerig maar net ‘n paar daggies oud gewees. So dit was ook vir my baie erg gewees. … jy kom in ‘n hospitaal - daar’s ‘n rooi zone daar’s ‘n groen zone… jy voel angstig.

(At one stage we went to a Covid-19 Hospital… because he needed polio drops. He was really only a few days old. So that was very difficult for me. You enter the hospital. There’s a red zone and a green zone. You feel anxious.)
Gary Reubenson
00:03:35:24 - 00:04:07:17
[...] parents and caregivers are understandably anxious about bringing their children and getting themselves to settings where they may acquire the virus. So it's quite possible that they may choose to wait in a month for most of the problem to resolve before they access what may seem to them to be relatively non urgent care.
VO
Paediatric specialist Dr Gary Reubenson says that although some parents claim they have been refused vaccinations by clinics, immunisation is usually available as an essential service. And for good reason: the WHO estimates that disruption to mass immunisation campaigns will leave more than 80 million infants at risk of preventable diseases.
Dr Gary Reubenson
00:05:00:07 - 00:05:40:06
[...] Measles is a very very infectious disease. Out of all that infectious diseases children are at risk for, it is probably the one that's most contagious. If they were to be an outbreak of a large outbreak of measles in a country like ours, children would die from that.
Prof Francois Venter
There are lessons from the Ebola epidemic in Central Africa where far more people died because of interruptions of the vaccine program than because of Ebola.
V/O


Both chronic care and immunisation face bigger challenges than patients’ fears: the pandemic could cause loss of funding to healthcare projects, and interruptions to essential supplies.
Dr Reubenson
00:14:22:23 - 00:14:23:11
We know that much of the drug manufacturing capacity in the world at the moment is localized to a few a few countries. And the ability to move those products around the world is compromised and the ability to get them into the country is potentially compromised and the ability to distribute them around the country is potentially compromised.
VO
The first shortages are already being reported.
Dr Bronwyn Bosch
00:11:48:22 - 00:12:26:17
the biggest thing that we're seeing now is shortages of PPE and we've seen hospitals around the country having to close temporarily because they don't have the right protective measures. That's the first thing. The second thing is all the chronic medications and contraception
VO
The domino effect on infant and maternal health will continue for months and even years to come.


00:12:26:19 - 00:13:01:08
The risk is that there are a lot of unplanned pregnancies into social circumstances where patients can't afford to have children.


Prof Francois Venter
I think we can anticipate in the next six months is a sudden surge in mortality amongst young women who are being forced into backstreet abortions because they got pregnant when they didn't have to.
VO
The message from experts is clear. Unless we act now and balance our response to the pandemic with the needs of our strained healthcare system, we are heading for a catastrophe.
Prof Francois Venter
00:14:14:16 - 00:14:44:05 [...] we have to get people back into the primary health care services in the next month or two or we really are going to see probably six months a year out of extended unnecessary death and disease.
Dr Bronwyn Bosch
00:17:15:18 - 00:17:37:18 [...] if we are setback it's going to take us many years to recuperate that ground that we've already gained which is really frightening and quite sad.
END










PROMO 1 11”
Closed clinics, patients defaulting on chronic medication, disruptions to supply chains and funding … How is our response to Covid-19 interfering with basic healthcare in South Africa?




PROMO 2 11”
As Coronavirus cases keep rising, many experts are worried that basic healthcare is falling by the wayside. How do we balance our covid response and effective routine medical care?




PROMO 3 11”
Fear of contracting Covid-19 is keeping many patients from accessing basic healthcare and many are defaulting on their chronic medication. Are we heading for a healthcare catastrophe?

People are scared of being taken away. So someone with onset symptoms for TB is not necessarily keen on being tested (in case it is Covid-19). On top of that, historic practices of forcefully sending patients with drug resistant TB to far away hospitals have also left its mark on communities. It's adding to the fear of being tested. TB medications are most effective if the disease is caught early, and treatment is not interrupted. Covid-19 poses obstacles for both. HIV Similar to TB, HIV is a major concern for sub-Saharan countries. South Africa has seen the biggest HIV epidemic in the world. 7.7 million people are living with HIV in SA, around 62% is estimated to be on ARV. A six-month interruption of supply of ARVs across the whole population of people living with HIV on treatment would be expected to lead to an approximately 2-fold increase in HIV-related deaths over a one year period compared to the case with no disruption. In sub-Saharan Africa this amounts to an excess of over 500,000 adult HIV deaths (including deaths of TB) should such a high level of disruption occur. The coronavirus pandemic could effectively set the clock on AIDS-related deaths back to 2008, when more than 950000 AIDS-related deaths were observed in the region. South Africa has made huge strides in the fight against HIV, particularly in recent years, but with Covid-19 in the neighbourhood the country will be forced backwards, and set targets will not be reached. When treatment is adhered to, a person’s HIV viral load drops to an undetectable level, keeping that person healthy and preventing onward transmission of the virus. When a person is unable to take antiretroviral therapy regularly, the viral load increases, impacting the person’s health, which can ultimately lead to death. Even relatively short-term interruptions to treatment can have a significant negative impact on a person’s health and potential to transmit HIV. Disrupted services could also reverse gains made in preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Since 2010, new HIV infections among children in sub-Saharan Africa have declined by 43%, from 250 000 in 2010 to 140 000 in 2018. NGO, Right to Care in Johannesburg, (Prof Ian Sanne) says that a high percentage of HIV-positive South Africans are missing their clinic appointments to collect their medication and testing for HIV has also dropped drastically due to fears of contracting Covid-19. The irony is that while people living with HIV really need their medication, they also need to avoid Covid-19 as their HIV status makes them particularly vulnerable. So, the dilemma for patients is whether to venture out on public transport and sit in crowded clinics for medication, or simply stay at home? There are some programmes emerging to help in this regard, Right to Care has designed and prototyped an ATM-like device. The pharmacy dispensing unit (PDU) will enable patients to visit locations that are convenient to them to pick up prescribed medication. All collected medications will be recorded against a central patient record. Some Clinics have also streamline processes to assist patients. Themba Lethu Clinic situated at Helen Joseph Hospital in Johannesburg has reduced the waiting time from 4 hours to 45 minutes for medication, according to Right to Care. There has also been a dramatic decrease in voluntary male circumcisions, which could accelerate the spread of HIV. Likewise more sporadic use of medication because someone with a higher viral load is more likely to infect another person with HIV. MATERNAL AND INFANT MORTALITY Unicef and the John Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health estimate that an additional 1.2 million children under the age of 5 could die because of a disruption in routine services like family planning, childbirth, postnatal care, and vaccinations. It is estimated that South Africa's current infant mortality rate is around 25.772 deaths per 1000 live births, and these numbers are significantly lower than in the past. Although SA has a bad track record when it comes to Maternal and Infant mortality, as a country we have made huge strides, specifically in cutting down the transmission rate of HIV infections from Mother to baby. As a country we have improved the health of mothers and babies, but with Covid-19 we could take a huge step backwards. Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital delivers about 60 babies every day. (According to a Wits University Study) The reality for most pregnant women in Soweto is that they are limited to and dependant on the hospital for all their pre- and postnatal care. Researchers found that while 20–25% of stillbirths occurred due to maternal medical conditions such as hypertension and diabetes, it also found that invasive bacterial infections were the immediate or underlying cause of death in 57.5% of all neonatal deaths. Overall, 74.4% of infection-related deaths were hospital-acquired, mainly due to multidrug-resistant bacteria. And this is all during “normal” times. Add Covid-19 to the mix and the situation begins to look dire for mothers and babies of Soweto. The economic downturn as a result of Covid-19 also plays a role in the maternal and infant mortality rates. Unicef reports that a one percent decrease in per capita GDP roughly correlates to a 0.3 percent increase in infant mortality, with girls at least twice as likely to be affected. The Measles and Rubella Partnership has estimated that more than 117 million children in 37 countries will miss out on their chance to be vaccinated for measles because mass campaigns and immunisation services will be suspended. Doctors Without Borders predict that 253,500 to 1.1 million additional children could die from preventable diseases. For every 1 adult life spared (COVID-19) an estimated 100 children could lose their lives. DIABETES Diabetes is another chronic illness that people need a constant medicine supply for, which can easily be disrupted by the health system being overstretched. At the moment there is no reported disruption in insulin supplies, but it difficulties would be inevitable as Covid-19 continues to demand focus from our medical world. An additional issue with all these chronic diseases is that it also makes the patient more vulnerable to Covid-19 itself. People with HIV and TB are at increased risk of contracting the disease itself, while people with diabetes are not more likely to get COVID-19 than the general population. The problem people with diabetes face is primarily a problem of worse outcomes, not greater chance of contracting the virus. And if your blood sugar levels are not controlled this makes it a lot worse. All the more reason for a steady/uninterrupted supply of medicine and care. BUT ITS NOT ALL DOOM AND GLOOM... there are some innovations that are being rolled out to assist patients in accessing their much-needed medications. -- like the Right ePharmacy Solutions, like Smart medicine lockers in key locations, and Pharmacy Dispensing Units (PDU's), which are basically medicine ATM's. -- There are also calls for government to supply patients with 6 months' HIV medication to limit the number of times the patient has to venture out and put himself at risk. Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 16 September 2020 Script: Healthcare Interrupted V/O For six months, the world’s attention has been on COVID-19. But our tunnel-vision-focus on one pandemic means we are sidelining others that have been with us much longer. Modelling by the World Health Organisation estimates that healthcare disruptions caused by the coronavirus could lead to 500 000 additional AIDS-related deaths between now and next year, with more than a 100% increase in new HIV infections amongst children. Malaria deaths could double, while the prevention and treatment of TB may be set back 5 to 8 years. Prof Francois Venter It's this weird thing in our society where people think all other illnesses have been suspended. People are getting older, they're getting other diseases like cancer and diabetes, they're getting HIV. V/O Prof Francois Venter is a veteran of South Africa’s long fight against HIV/AIDS. He has first-hand knowledge of how many decades of frontline research and lobbying lie behind our recent successes. Prof Francois Venter We really have made unbelievable gains with the HIV program both in terms of treatment and prevention. The TB programme as well has enjoyed for the first time in decades such success in the last three or four years. V/O South Africa is also enjoying hard-won gains in the fight against maternal and neonatal death rates. But now all this is at risk of being eroded, and we face a looming catastrophe in our already strained healthcare system - one that will cost our embattled economy and divided population dearly. LINK Millions of South Africans are on chronic medication for hypertension to HIV, tuberculosis and even diabetes. These people need to diligently take their medication regularly, especially since it’s believed that they are more vulnerable to the coronavirus. VO But when the country entered hard lockdown in March, that became easier said than done. Siyabonga I’m HIV+ since from birth... VO In December, eighteen year-old Siyabonga and his brother fled their abusive home in Limpopo and found refuge here at Soweto-based NGO, iKageng. Only a few months later, things went from bad to worse as the pandemic took hold. Siyabonga I tried to go for medication but I didn’t reach for that goal. Claire: Why? Because I went here in Mandela Sisulu and I found the other woman, and I tried to explain the story, eish Ma’am I don’t have a transfer from the clinic but I’m looking for at least treatment. The lady replied, no we can’t give you treatment. VO In the turmoil of escaping Limpopo, he left behind the documents that would allow him to access his ARV treatment in Gauteng. Siyabonga That’s the only thing that I forgot there in Limpopo. I took all the things, even the transfer from the school but I forgot that one. VO Siyabonga endured two months without treatment - until iKageng intervened on his behalf in late May. Dr Bronwyn Bosch As soon as you're not taking your ARVs the HIV can multiply in the blood and overpower the immune system. VO Dr Bronwyn Bosch of Ezintsha explains that although it is different for every patient, treatment disruptions are worrisome. Bronwyn Bosch Any interruptions in treatment whether it's a day or a month or a year, the HIV if there is any ARV or be in the blood it can become resistant to those ARVs. So the regimen that you're on may not necessarily work anymore. V/O As we entered lockdown, most non-essential medical care was suspended. Specialised clinics were closed, elective surgeries delayed, and services scaled down to ready the system for COVID-19. But it is becoming clear that lockdown is not the only factor preventing people from accessing healthcare… Phumzile I’m scared, because it kills, so I am scared. VO Single mother Phumzile Kubheka relies on hypertension medication and ARVs. But for her, the threat of the coronavirus looms larger than her chronic conditions. Phumzile If I die after I go to the clinic who will my children be left with, because to them I'm everything. I live alone with them in this house, so yes it is scary. V/O Phumzile is not alone. Most healthcare sectors - public and private - are reporting a decrease in patients seeking routine care. People are staying away from clinics and hospitals, especially the elderly and those with chronic conditions, labelled as “Covid Co-morbidities”, says Gloria Sibeko of iKageng. Gloria Even grannies, grannies will stay with such high hypertension knowing very well that I’m not feeling okay. Prof Francois Venter We're seeing a dramatic drop in TB testing across the country. And we're seeing a decrease in pick-ups for antiretrovirals. VO For those who do seek care, Covid infection control measures can lengthen waiting times. Phumzile 18:03:37:05 I left my house at 5 o’clock.I went to the clinic and stood there til around 9am. Gloria they have to wait out of the clinic, and queue out of, and maintain social distancing… VO When it comes to chronic medication at least, there is one solution that minimizes contact, queuing time, and the risk of infection. Link When you think of postboxes you think of something from yesteryear but in these challenging times perhaps we should look to the past for inspiration. VO Adapting existing technology and innovations, Right ePharmacy is rolling out “Collect and Go” medicine lockers at 70 sites across Gauteng, Mpumalanga and the Free State. Fanie - Right to Care They can just basically come to the locker, they put in their unique pin. The locker opens, you take your medicine and you go on with your normal day. V/O Right ePharmacy also has ATM Pharmacies, known as PDU’s at various locations in Johannesburg, and in Bloemfontein, explains managing director, Fanie Hendriksz. Fanie - Right to Care So the benefits, you can see we’re in a community shopping centre, so people are now aligning their medicine collection with the onthly or weekly or daily shopping. It’s close to a taxi route. V/O The units operate 7 days a week and patients connect “real time” with a pharmacist who can advise them if they have any concerns. Behind the interface is a stock room where a robotic arm selects the appropriate medication, labels it and dispenses it to the patient. Fanie - Right to Care We’ve seen that the collection time is under 3 minutes - and that means 2 months’ supply and a live interaction with the pharmacist. V/O Taking strain off public clinics and hospitals will improve access to treatment for non-COVID patients. But for some services, there’s no avoiding human contact. Link Most experts agree that children aren’t as severely affected by Covid-19 directly as adults and the elderly. But the real concern is the indirect repercussions of the pandemic. Anne Kahts Dit is baie angstig om uit te gaan, veral met ‘n piep babatjie. (It is very unnerving to go out, especially with a small infant.) VO Anné Kats gave birth to a baby boy at the beginning of May. Navigating lockdown with a newborn has exacerbated the anxiety of being a new mother. Anné Kahts Ons was op ‘n deel was ons na ‘n Covid-19 hospitaal toe - wat uitgesit is vir Covid-19 pasiente, want hy moes sy polio drops gaan kry het. Hy was rerig maar net ‘n paar daggies oud gewees. So dit was ook vir my baie erg gewees. … jy kom in ‘n hospitaal - daar’s ‘n rooi zone daar’s ‘n groen zone… jy voel angstig. (At one stage we went to a Covid-19 Hospital… because he needed polio drops. He was really only a few days old. So that was very difficult for me. You enter the hospital. There’s a red zone and a green zone. You feel anxious.) Gary Reubenson 00:03:35:24 - 00:04:07:17 [...] parents and caregivers are understandably anxious about bringing their children and getting themselves to settings where they may acquire the virus. So it's quite possible that they may choose to wait in a month for most of the problem to resolve before they access what may seem to them to be relatively non urgent care. VO Paediatric specialist Dr Gary Reubenson says that although some parents claim they have been refused vaccinations by clinics, immunisation is usually available as an essential service. And for good reason: the WHO estimates that disruption to mass immunisation campaigns will leave more than 80 million infants at risk of preventable diseases. Dr Gary Reubenson 00:05:00:07 - 00:05:40:06 [...] Measles is a very very infectious disease. Out of all that infectious diseases children are at risk for, it is probably the one that's most contagious. If they were to be an outbreak of a large outbreak of measles in a country like ours, children would die from that. Prof Francois Venter There are lessons from the Ebola epidemic in Central Africa where far more people died because of interruptions of the vaccine program than because of Ebola. V/O Both chronic care and immunisation face bigger challenges than patients’ fears: the pandemic could cause loss of funding to healthcare projects, and interruptions to essential supplies. Dr Reubenson 00:14:22:23 - 00:14:23:11 We know that much of the drug manufacturing capacity in the world at the moment is localized to a few a few countries. And the ability to move those products around the world is compromised and the ability to get them into the country is potentially compromised and the ability to distribute them around the country is potentially compromised. VO The first shortages are already being reported. Dr Bronwyn Bosch 00:11:48:22 - 00:12:26:17 the biggest thing that we're seeing now is shortages of PPE and we've seen hospitals around the country having to close temporarily because they don't have the right protective measures. That's the first thing. The second thing is all the chronic medications and contraception VO The domino effect on infant and maternal health will continue for months and even years to come. 00:12:26:19 - 00:13:01:08 The risk is that there are a lot of unplanned pregnancies into social circumstances where patients can't afford to have children. Prof Francois Venter I think we can anticipate in the next six months is a sudden surge in mortality amongst young women who are being forced into backstreet abortions because they got pregnant when they didn't have to. VO The message from experts is clear. Unless we act now and balance our response to the pandemic with the needs of our strained healthcare system, we are heading for a catastrophe. Prof Francois Venter 00:14:14:16 - 00:14:44:05 [...] we have to get people back into the primary health care services in the next month or two or we really are going to see probably six months a year out of extended unnecessary death and disease. Dr Bronwyn Bosch 00:17:15:18 - 00:17:37:18 [...] if we are setback it's going to take us many years to recuperate that ground that we've already gained which is really frightening and quite sad. END PROMO 1 11” Closed clinics, patients defaulting on chronic medication, disruptions to supply chains and funding … How is our response to Covid-19 interfering with basic healthcare in South Africa? PROMO 2 11” As Coronavirus cases keep rising, many experts are worried that basic healthcare is falling by the wayside. How do we balance our covid response and effective routine medical care? PROMO 3 11” Fear of contracting Covid-19 is keeping many patients from accessing basic healthcare and many are defaulting on their chronic medication. Are we heading for a healthcare catastrophe?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Many routine, yet essential healthcare services are impacted on by Covid-19
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The world is focussing on Covid-19, and the devastating effects on humanity, but experts are warning that there are other humanitarian crises waiting in the wings. Thousands of people across South Africa depend on regular access to medicine and healthcare, patients with HIV, TB, Diabetes, Heart Disease to name but a few... but Covid-19 is disrupting more and more of the healthcare services that these people depend on. From being harassed by police on their way to the clinic, to being too scared to seek medical help, or to collect medicines... it is becoming evident that we're faced with an imminent disaster.
metadata.Summary: Covid-19 has disrupted our lives in many ways. Businesses have closed, people have lost livelihoods, loved ones... The world as we knew it just a few months ago has changed forever. One important, sometimes overlooked, impact is the disruption in routine medical services across the world. Reports from many countries show severe disruption of routine healthcare services in many countries due to lockdowns imposed, diversion of healthcare workforce to COVID-19 response, and disruption of travel and supply chains. Even basic immunization services have come to a grinding halt in many settings. Internationally the Irish National Breast Screening Programme (Breast Check) reports 0 mammograms for the month of April, and a 96% reduction in samples sent to CervicalCheck labs. In the USA, the American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association warn that emergency rooms across the country are 40 to 50% less busy when it comes to cardiovascular patients seeking care. People are staying home, ignoring serious symptoms for fear of contracting Covid-19. New figures from University College London suggest there could be 18,000 more cancer deaths in England because of the coronavirus pandemic. A similar situation is playing off in Sub-Saharan Africa. Besides cancer and heart disease we have a set of medical challenges that cannot simply be ignored until we find a vaccine for Covid-19. Prof Sanne (Right to Care) told News24 there had been an increase in missed appointments by HIV patients of between 40% and 60% since the lockdown, and a similar issue was expected for diabetes and other illnesses needing chronic medication.
